title: “掌握自己的命运风险更小”——离开 3A 大厂的开发者们
content:
"It's less risky to be the masters of our own fate" – The AAA developers going indie | GamesIndustry.biz

Justin Fischer and Brock Feldman suddenly found themselves out of a job in 2025, when Warner Bros decided to shutter their studio, Player First Games, the developer of Multiversus.
The free-to-play fighting game, which featured various Warner Bros characters, had launched in beta in 2022 before going offline around a year later, in preparation for the full launch in May 2024. Warner
acquired Player First
just after that 1.0 launch – then announced
the studio's closure
seven months later, after
pulling the plug on Multiversus
.
Fischer says that there's no secret around why the game shut down. "It's just user acquisition costs are hard for everybody," he tells
GamesIndustry.biz
. "Free-to-play has been taking a beating, and it wasn't just Multiversus… The economy of the industry is changing, and it's hard out there for everybody."
The story is a depressingly familiar one. It's estimated that there have been
more than 58,000 layoffs in the games industry since 2022
, with the majority occurring in North America. The AAA sector has been particularly hard hit. "I think this is as bad as the '83 crash if you're a game developer based in North America or western Europe, in a traditional AAA studio," said 1UP Ventures' Amir Satvat in a recent feature in
Edge magazine
. "That is ground zero for destruction."
Many of those leaving the AAA sector – Fischer and Feldman included – have sought refuge in the indie space, and
GamesIndustry.biz
has spoken to developers who have made the leap from AAA to indie in recent years to find out their experiences. The pay cut can be considerable, and the risk of failure in such a crowded market is high. Yet with so few jobs remaining in AAA, for many there is little choice but to go indie – although the relative freedom can be empowering.
Reach for the stars
Fischer and Feldman formed Airlock Games last year, and they are currently working on the sci-fi horror management sim
What the Stars Forgot
. Fischer says that in such a competitive environment, with user acquisition costs "through the roof" it made more sense to them to start with something small, rather than attempting to raise "$30 million to do a massive multiplayer competitive game."
What The Stars Forgot is a spaceship management sim  |
Image credit:
Airlock Games
The idea was to focus on a concept they could make quickly and that they were passionate about, instead of trying to cater to the largest possible audience. "We can fail fast," says Fischer, referring to the oft-quoted tech industry maxim, adding that they wanted to do something that felt realistic with the current state of the industry.
Importantly, they're having fun. "For me personally, it's been the best time I've had games in a long time making them, and the most fun I've had, and the most energised I feel," says Fischer. He says that as you become more senior in the games industry, you tend to be put in a "box" and end up working only on one specific area of expertise. But after years of being boxed in as a producer, Fischer now gets to dabble in things like audio and dialogue. "I get to work a lot of sides of my brain every day, and that just is really satisfying, really engaging, really fun."
Airlock Games has deliberately created a small scope for its debut title. "Brock and I are very good at figuring out scope," says Fischer, "and we've had conversations multiple times where usually it's me saying, 'Hey, you want to have this idea?' And he's like, 'That's awesome: that's game six'." The idea is to start something they can finish in a reasonable amount of time, rather than getting lost down a "rabbit hole of content".
"We can't control what the publisher scene looks like, but we can control what we're making"
Fischer and Feldman are also aware that now is a terrible time to be looking for investors, with most of them having moved on to things like AI after pouring money into the games industry during the COVID era. That's why they're intending to ship What the Stars Forgot "without a dollar of investment".
"Brock and I both have authority issues, so we'd like to not sell parts of the company and just be able to totally bootstrap this ourselves," says Fischer. "It's the one thing totally in our control. I can't control what the investment environment looks like, we can't control what the publisher scene looks like, but we can control what we're making, and how we ship it, and how we communicate with an audience."
That said, Airlock Games is happy to have conversations with "interesting partners who want to help us on this journey", and the firm raised over $25,000 in a
Kickstarter campaign for What the Stars Forgot
last year. Otherwise, though, the pair are getting by on their severance pay from Warner Bros.

"It's definitely scrappy," says Fischer. "It's bootstrap for sure. But at the moment, it's been nice to just focus on making something and not having to worry about the investment side, not having to worry about a big corporate hierarchy that you have to answer to."
The pair are more than aware of the risks involved in going it alone and the difficulty of standing out in such a crowded marketplace. But they're not doing it to get rich. "Success level one is Brock and I get to keep doing this," explains Fischer. "Success level two is we get to keep doing this and we get to grow. Success level three is we're millionaires. And Brock and I are much more interested in the first two at the moment."
Better than doomscrolling
Murray Pannell has worked in marketing and publishing for decades at a number of huge games companies, including Electronic Arts, Xbox, PlayStation, and Ubisoft. "I've done the rounds, that's for sure," he tells
GamesIndustry.biz
.
